extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, potential authors, and academic stakeholders interested in mathematical journal publishing and open-access models
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and policy summary for authors considering submitting to the new Forum of Mathematics journals (Pi and Sigma): explains scope, editorial process, fees/waivers, format, and transfer policies. Useful for authors choosing where and how to submit mathematical research under a gold open-access model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold open access / publication-charge model
rubrics_metrics.description: All articles will be freely available without subscription charges, but authors, upon their paper being accepted, be asked to pay a publication charge to cover costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication charges will be set at zero for the first three years, and then raised to somewhere around £500 GBP or $750 USD after the initial three-year period (with fee waivers available for authors from developing countries). The post notes the possibility of obtaining additional funding (e.g. philanthropic organisations) which may allow for fee reductions or additional waivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial decisions independent of ability to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions will not be influenced by the author’s ability to pay for the charges; the charges only come into effect if the paper is accepted for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation is emphasised to reassure authors; commenters expand that fee waivers should be handled administratively (so editors/referees do not know the payment status) to avoid bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic-only publishing / print-on-demand
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal will be purely electronic, with physical issues available on a print-on-demand basis only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping the journal electronic helps keep costs low, and removes hard constraints on annual page counts so acceptance decisions will not be influenced by backlog or fixed page budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: No artificial page/backlog constraints affecting acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the journal is electronic with print-on-demand, there is no hard constraint on how many or how few pages will be published each year, so acceptance decisions will not be influenced by artificial constraints such as the size of the journal backlog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a benefit compared with traditional journals that may reject or delay work for space reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and dual-structure: Pi (flagship) vs Sigma (specialist clusters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forum of Mathematics is a complex consisting of a generalist flagship journal (Forum of Mathematics, Pi) and a specialist journal (Forum of Mathematics, Sigma) organised into 'clusters' for major subfields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pi is intended as a top-tier journal accepting significant papers of interest to a wide audience (comparable to JAMS, Inventiones, Annals), while Sigma functions as a collection of specialist journals (analysis, topology, algebra, discrete math, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability between journals/clusters with retention of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be possible to easily transfer a submission between journals or clusters while retaining all the referee reports and other editorial data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism aims to reduce the need for authors to start over with new submissions and new referee reports when a paper is deemed out of scope for one part of the Forum. However, a submission can still be rejected entirely if unsuitable for both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard editorial workflow (submission → refereeing → decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers are submitted by authors, sent out to referees by the editors, and (if accepted) published by the Forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Forum otherwise functions like a regular mathematics journal in terms of peer review and editorial responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should aim submissions appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are expected to aim their submission at the most appropriate location (Pi or the right Sigma cluster) to reduce the time and effort expended on processing the paper by everyone involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although transfers are possible, selecting the right venue first helps avoid unnecessary delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-waiver policy for authors without funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Fee waivers will be available for authors who can demonstrate that they do not have access to appropriate funds for paying the publication charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to avoid creating barriers to publishing for researchers from developing countries or those without funding; commenters discuss institutional/library subscription models as an alternative way to provide waivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher-provided services justify part of the charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Cambridge University Press will provide paid staff to handle typesetting, web design, publicity, and administrative tasks; publication charges pay for these services rather than the scholarly labour of referees/editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post contrasts this paid-staff model with volunteer-run journals, arguing paid employees can improve scalability and stability; commenters debate whether those services justify the proposed fee levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of costs and potential alternative funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication charges are not entirely fixed; the possibility of obtaining additional funding (e.g. philanthropic organisations or institutional support) may allow fee reductions or waivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes that more transparent cost breakdowns could affect fee levels and that library subscriptions or institutional funding could be used for waivers or lower charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clusters are primarily administrative; Sigma is unified
rubrics_metrics.description: Clusters in Sigma are mostly for internal administrative purposes; Sigma is to be treated as essentially a unified journal with clusters as secondary designations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers spanning multiple clusters can be handled by different sets of editors; clusters help assign editors and referees without rigidly partitioning content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aiming to compete on price and quality, not 'gaming' rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forum aims to obtain high-quality papers that will be well cited, but will not try to 'game' citation indices and journal rankings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The long-term goal is to reduce community dependence on simplistic metrics and to build reputation by publishing strong work rather than manipulating indices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of author rights (no onerous copyright transfer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The discussion and comments emphasise moving away from the practice of making authors sign over their copyrights (FAQ indicates more author-friendly copyright arrangements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters regard retention of copyright by authors as a positive feature of the model; authors should check the FAQ/publisher policy for exact license terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of editorial and administrative roles to preserve integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational tasks like fee handling, waivers, and administrative correspondence are separated from editorial decisions so that editors and referees do not base decisions on payment status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters suggest handling waivers administratively (editors not informed of waiver status) to guard against biased decisions; this is presented as a safeguard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability vs volunteer-run journals tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: The post argues that while very low-cost volunteer-run journals exist, having some paid services helps journals scale and remain stable (volunteer labour can be unavailable or transient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are asked to weigh the tradeoffs between minimal-cost volunteer journals (e.g., JMLR, Electronic Journal of Combinatorics) and a model with modest publication charges that fund paid support staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial governance and visible editorial board
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forum will have an editorial board (Rob Kirby as managing editor, thirteen other editors including Tim Gowers and Terence Tao, and a board of associate editors in formation) and an FAQ already in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A named editorial board and transparency about governance are presented as credibility factors for authors deciding where to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open experimentation and plurality of publishing models
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forum is framed as an experiment in moving away from traditional subscription models; it is presented as one of several possible alternatives rather than the unique solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post encourages experimentation with different publishing models to discover viable alternatives to the status quo and stresses coexistence with other models (subscription, volunteer-run OA, institutional funding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-competition argument for author-side charges
rubrics_metrics.description: One argued benefit of a publication-charge (author-pay) model is greater price competition visible to authors (authors can compare publication charges), while libraries are often forced into bundled subscriptions that obscure costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This economic argument is offered to justify author-side charges as a mechanism to discipline overall publishing pricing.
